readings.title: Five Children and It: a gold-fish morning (Chapter III, first part)
readings.challenge: Follow a conversation that keeps being interrupted, and hold on to the argument underneath it.
readings.focus: After two disappointing wishes, the children argue about whether the Psammead can be trusted and what a sensible wish would be.
readings.context: Five Children and It (1902) is by the English writer E. Nesbit. Cyril, Anthea (called Panther), Robert and Jane, with their baby brother the Lamb, are spending the summer in the Kent countryside, where they have dug up a Psammead: a grumpy, furry sand-fairy that grants one wish a day. Every wish lasts only until sunset. Their first two wishes, to be “beautiful as the day” and to have boundless wealth, both went wrong. Martha is the nursemaid looking after them while their parents are away. Two-shilling pieces were silver coins, and fifty pounds was a great deal of money. “Dead Sea fish” is Jane’s muddle of “Dead Sea fruit,” a fruit said to look lovely and turn to ashes.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Being Wanted,” from the opening until Martha sends the Baby with them; opens “The morning after the children had been the possessors of boundless wealth, and had been…”; closes “…Martha caught them at the gate, and insisted on their taking the Baby with them.”.

questions.prompt: Why is it so hard to talk about the Psammead at breakfast? Find two things the Baby does.
facilitatorNotes: He hangs by his head through the bar of his high chair, hits Cyril with a spoon, demands jam (“nam”) and finally tips over the bowl of gold-fish. The broken-off sentences in the dialogue show the talk being cut short again and again.
evidence: hit Cyril heavily on the head with it
the bowl of golden carp in the middle of the table rolled on its side

questions.prompt: Robert thinks the Psammead is “a spiteful brute”; Cyril disagrees. Whose explanation of the first two wishes makes more sense to you?
facilitatorNotes: Robert suspects the fairy wishes their wishes to do no good; Cyril blames the children for choosing badly. Both can be argued, but Cyril’s fits a fairy that grants exactly what is asked.
evidence: I feel almost sure it wishes every time that our wishes shan't do us any good
it was silly to wish for boundless wealth

questions.prompt: The narrator often stops to talk to the reader, about biting off thread or about “lending ears.” Find one of these asides. What does it add?
facilitatorNotes: The asides make the narrator a joking grown-up on the reader’s side, who even admits to “getting too instructive.” Some readers enjoy them; others may feel they slow the story. Both responses are fair.
evidence: Now what is one to believe--what with nurses and science?
but I fear I am getting too instructive

questions.prompt: Why does Martha’s “It’s not respectable” end the argument about Jane’s petticoat?
facilitatorNotes: The petticoat is as pretty as a frock, but Martha’s word is law, and the narrator jokes that once a grown-up says “not respectable” there is nothing more to say.
evidence: Martha's word was law
And when people say that, it's no use anyone's saying anything.

readings.title: Five Children and It: Robert’s cross wish (Chapter III, second part)
readings.challenge: Notice how a wish can be made by accident, and decide who is to blame.
readings.focus: Robert’s angry words become a wish, and the Psammead will not take it back.
readings.context: Recap: after a breakfast upset by the Lamb and a bowl of gold-fish, the children agreed to wish for fifty pounds in two-shilling pieces. Martha has made them take the Baby to the gravel-pit. Ginger-beer is a fizzy drink; a Plesiosaurus, an Ichthyosaurus and a Megatherium are prehistoric animals.
readings.contentNote: The Psammead tells a comic tale of a Stone Age boy who wished he was dead, and was, until sunset.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Being Wanted,” from Martha at the gate until the children mark the Psammead’s hiding place; opens “"Not want him indeed! Why, everybody 'ud want him, a duck! with all their hearts they…”; closes “The children marked the spot with a ring of stones.”.

questions.prompt: What did the children forget to do the day before, and why does it matter now?
facilitatorNotes: They ran from the falling gold without marking the Psammead’s place with a ring of stones, so now they cannot find it. At the end of this part they make sure to mark it.
evidence: they had not had time to mark the spot where the Psammead was
The children marked the spot with a ring of stones.

questions.prompt: Why does Robert say, “I only wish everybody did want him with all their hearts”? Why is this a dangerous sentence here?
facilitatorNotes: He is hot and cross after the sand, the ginger-beer and the howling, and speaks without thinking. But the Psammead is close by, and any wish spoken near it may come true.
evidence: I only wish everybody did want him with all their hearts
Robert, usually a very patient brother, so far forgot himself

questions.prompt: After Robert speaks there is a silence. What is everyone waiting for?
facilitatorNotes: They are waiting for him to say he is sorry. He knows he has been “rather like a pig,” which is why he answers the Psammead sulkily. Ask whether the narrator’s description of this kind of silence matches readers’ own experience.
evidence: waits for the one who oughtn't to have said it is sorry
because he knew he had been behaving rather like a pig

questions.prompt: The Psammead will not take the wish back. Is its story of the prehistoric boy a fair answer to Jane?
facilitatorNotes: Its point is that wishes spoken in a temper still count: “You ought to be careful what you do wish.” Some readers will think it fair to keep to the rules; others will think it unkind, since Robert did not really mean it.
evidence: chopping and changing--it's not business
You ought to be careful what you do wish.

readings.title: Five Children and It: the lady in the carriage (Chapter III, third part)
readings.challenge: Notice how characters show themselves through the way they talk.
readings.focus: The wish works at once: a grand lady, a coachman and a footman all want the Lamb.
readings.context: Recap: Robert crossly wished that everybody wanted the Baby, and the Psammead granted it; the wish lasts until sunset. The children set off home. A coachman drives a carriage, and a groom or footman rides beside him as a servant. A lodge is a gatehouse; a stile is a step over a fence; brake-fern is bracken.
readings.contentNote: A lady drives off with the baby without asking, and her two servants come to blows over him.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Being Wanted,” from the walk home until the children escape with the Lamb; opens “"We may as well get along home," said Robert. "I'll say I'm sorry; but anyway if it's no…”; closes “…road on the left, they took courage, and the road, Anthea carrying the sleeping Lamb.”.

questions.prompt: How does Lady Chittenden describe herself, and what does that tell you about her?
facilitatorNotes: She mentions her photograph in the papers and that she is called a Beauty, then says it is “all nonsense,” which is a way of boasting while pretending not to. She holds the Lamb “very awkwardly” before simply taking him.
evidence: They call me a Beauty, you know, but of course that's all nonsense.
held him very awkwardly, as if she was not used to babies

questions.prompt: What does the coachman say about his mistress, and why do the hidden children exchange “uncomfortable glances”?
facilitatorNotes: He says she “hates kids,” so her sudden wish to adopt the Lamb can only be the Psammead’s doing. Then the servants start planning to keep him themselves, and the children see how dangerous the wish is.
evidence: Hates kids. Got none of her own, and can't abide other folkses'.
exchanged uncomfortable glances

questions.prompt: How does Cyril rescue the Lamb, and what makes his plan work?
facilitatorNotes: He waits until the two men are fighting, creeps round the far side, takes the sleeping baby and hides with the others in the fern. The quarrel the wish caused is exactly what gives him his chance.
evidence: the two men were far too much occupied with their quarrel to notice anything
covered by high strong-scented brake-fern

readings.title: Five Children and It: the camp by the road (Chapter III, fourth part)
readings.challenge: Watch a character think fast under pressure, and work out his plan before the others do.
readings.focus: Cyril keeps the Lamb safe by playing for time until sunset.
readings.context: Recap: everyone who sees the Lamb wants him until sunset. The children have escaped a grand lady who drove off with him and are hurrying home. Faggots are bundles of sticks; a stone-breaker broke stones for road-making; paraffin is lamp oil.
readings.contentNote: Nesbit’s Romani characters are called “gipsies,” as was usual in 1902; many Romani people now consider the word offensive. The scene draws on an old, false story that Roma steal children, and their speech is spelled to sound uneducated. The children also frighten a little girl away with a threat about bears.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Being Wanted,” from the walk home until the sun goes behind the hill; opens “Adventures dogged their footsteps. A boy with a bundle of faggots on his back dropped his…”; closes “…the sun sets; she has to do it too, to the minute, or they would know the reason why!”.

questions.prompt: How do the children protect the Lamb on the road? Are any of their methods unkind?
facilitatorNotes: They refuse to hand him over, threaten a boy with their fists, hide in the hedge, and Cyril tells a crying little girl that bears will eat her. Readers may judge the threat cruel, even though the children are frightened for the Baby.
evidence: So that bears can come and eat you as soon as it gets dark
to hide in the hedge whenever they saw anyone coming

questions.prompt: Cyril says, “You shall have him if you want him.” Why does he say it, and why does Anthea misunderstand?
facilitatorNotes: He is playing for time, since the wish ends at sunset, and he whispers the plan. Anthea hears only the words and cries out. The others then admire his cleverness.
evidence: Sunset! we'll get away then.
filled with wonder and admiration at his having been so clever

questions.prompt: Robert offers to fetch dinner from home. What is his secret plan, and how do the men see through it?
facilitatorNotes: He means to bring help. They guess he would bring the police, and “D’jever catch a weasel asleep?” means they are too sharp to be fooled.
evidence: They did not know his thoughtful secret intention. But the gipsies did in a minute.
D'jever catch a weasel asleep?

questions.prompt: By the end of the afternoon, how have the children’s feelings about the camp changed?
facilitatorNotes: Robert said the dinner would choke him, but they all ate it; Anthea says the people are not unkind; the children even enjoy showing off the Lamb. The people they meet are kinder than the danger they feared.
evidence: they aren't unkind people, or they wouldn't be going to give us any dinner
they were all glad enough to take what they could get

readings.title: Five Children and It: sunset at last (Chapter III, end)
readings.challenge: Decide whether the moral the narrator states matches what happened.
readings.focus: The wish ends, a Romani woman gives the Lamb her blessing, and the children find out what they really feel.
readings.context: Recap: because of the wish, the people at the roadside camp all want the Lamb, and Cyril has promised to hand him over at bedtime, knowing the wish will end at sunset. Now the sun is slow to set.
readings.contentNote: Nesbit’s Romani characters are called “gipsies,” as was usual in 1902; many Romani people now consider the word offensive. The scene draws on an old, false story that Roma steal children, and their speech is spelled to sound uneducated.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Being Wanted,” from the gipsies’ impatience to the end of the chapter; opens “But the gipsies were getting impatient.”; closes “…I hope this doesn't often happen, but I daresay it has happened sometimes, even to you!”.

questions.prompt: How does Anthea try to gain time, and how does the Lamb help?
facilitatorNotes: She pours out every detail of his baths, toys and meals. The Lamb stops roaring to listen and then tells the woman “G’way, ugsie!”
evidence: anything to gain time
he has a crockery rabbit to go into the warm bath with him

questions.prompt: The narrator compares sunset to an “invisible sponge.” What does it wipe away, and how do the adults behave afterwards?
facilitatorNotes: It wipes away the anxious wanting and leaves them muddled and blank. Then each politely refuses the Baby, as if embarrassed.
evidence: as if some invisible sponge had wiped away these cross and anxious expressions
I shouldn't like to deprive you, miss

questions.prompt: Amelia still looks kindly at the Lamb after sunset. Why might that be, and what does she say about her people?
facilitatorNotes: She has “lost all mine,” so her feeling for a baby is her own and not the wish’s. She also says her people do not steal babies, which answers the stereotype the scene began with. Robert thinks she talked rot; the others think her kind.
evidence: Us gipsies don't steal babies, whatever they may tell you when you're naughty.
But I've lost all mine.

questions.prompt: The narrator says she “did not mean it to have a moral.” What is the moral, and did the story earn it?
facilitatorNotes: That you value a brother or sister most when you might lose them; Robert says everything looked different then. The joke about “nasty forward” morals lets the narrator teach a lesson while pretending not to.
evidence: everything looked so different when we thought we were going to lose him
morals are nasty forward beings

readings.title: Five Children and It: a castle where the house was (Chapter VI, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice how a wish goes wrong when it is made in a hurry, and follow a character who arrives late to the trouble.
readings.focus: Robert’s careless wish lets the others wish without him, and he comes home to find a castle under siege.
readings.context: Five Children and It (1902) is by the English writer E. Nesbit. Cyril, Anthea (called Panther), Robert and Jane, with their baby brother the Lamb, are spending the summer in the Kent countryside, where they have dug up a Psammead: a grumpy, furry sand-fairy that grants one wish a day. Every wish lasts only until sunset. Yesterday they wished for wings, and the trouble that followed brought them home very late, so Martha, the nursemaid, is keeping them indoors as a punishment. Only Robert may go out for half an hour to fetch the day’s wish. To “lick Simpkins Minor” means to beat a schoolfellow in a fight. A besieged castle is surrounded by an enemy army. The soldiers talk like knights in old adventure books: “By my halidom” is an oath, a varlet or knave is a servant boy, garb means clothes, belike means probably, hither means here and yonder means over there. Lancet windows are tall and narrow; battlements are the notched tops of castle walls.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “A Castle and No Dinner,” from the opening until Robert is taken to the leader; opens “The others were to be kept in as a punishment for the misfortunes of the day before. Of…”; closes “And to the leader Robert was dragged forthwith--by the reluctant ear.”.

questions.prompt: Why can’t Robert think of a good wish? What does he wish by accident?
facilitatorNotes: Only small things for himself come into his head, such as candy, a stamp album or a knife. Stuck, he wishes the Psammead could give one of the others their wish without their coming to ask, and it does, so the others wish while he is away.
evidence: nothing would come into his head but little things for himself
I wish you could give one of the others their wish without their having to come here to ask for it. Oh, don't!

questions.prompt: How does Robert work out what the others have wished? Which details tell him?
facilitatorNotes: The house and railings are gone; a black castle with battlements and towers stands in their place, and tents and men in armor fill the garden. He guesses at once that they wished for a castle and that it is being besieged.
evidence: there was no house to be seen
They've wished for a castle, and it's being besieged!

questions.prompt: Robert has read many “historical romances for the young.” How do they help him with the soldiers, and where do they let him down?
facilitatorNotes: He knows “varlet” is not meant rudely and can translate their old-fashioned speech in his head, but he answers “Over there” instead of “Yonder!” The joke is that knowing the books is not the same as being in one.
evidence: It was the way people talked in historical romances for the young, he knew
directly he had said it he knew he ought to have said "Yonder!"

questions.prompt: Robert does not run from the two soldiers. Was standing still brave, sensible, or both?
facilitatorNotes: He stays because his legs are short and running might annoy them; the soldiers call him brave, and being called brave makes him feel brave. Readers can argue that sensible caution was taken for courage, and that it then grew into the real thing.
evidence: Robert remembered the shortness of his own legs and did not run away
Robert felt pleased at being called brave, and somehow it made him feel brave.

readings.title: Five Children and It: Sir Wulfric de Talbot (Chapter VI, second part)
readings.challenge: Enjoy a joke built on two ways of talking, and notice when the reader understands more than the characters.
readings.focus: Robert tries to explain the Psammead to a knight who is himself part of a wish.
readings.context: Recap: Robert’s accidental wish let the others wish while he was out. They wished for a castle, and he came back to find it surrounded by an army; two soldiers have dragged him by the ear to their leader. A crest is a decoration on top of a helmet and a cuirass is a breastplate; heraldry is the study of coats of arms. Nesbit jokes that the knight’s armor mixes many centuries, like the pictures in cheap adventure books. Scathe means harm; grammercy means thank you; “beshrew thee” is a mild curse; sooth means truth; succor means help; to wend is to go. “Ripping” was schoolboy slang for excellent.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “A Castle and No Dinner,” from Robert’s meeting with the leader until he wishes himself back with the others; opens “The leader was the most glorious creature Robert had ever seen. He was exactly like the…”; closes “…consciousness for an instant. When he opened his eyes the others were crowding round him.”.

questions.prompt: What is mixed up about Sir Wulfric’s armor and camp? Why doesn’t Robert notice?
facilitatorNotes: The shield, sword, breastplate and helmet come from different centuries, and the tents are modern army tents. Robert knows no more about it than the artists who draw the adventure-book pictures, so it all looks perfectly correct to him. The narrator is teasing both the boy and the books.
evidence: His armor and his weapons were all, I am almost sure, of quite different periods.
he knew no more of heraldry or archaeology than the gifted artists

questions.prompt: Robert tries to talk like a boy in an old romance. Find a place where his everyday words break through. How does the knight react?
facilitatorNotes: He starts grandly and slips straight into “The fact is, it's like this”; later “ripping” and “fix” puzzle the knight, who guesses a fix is a fray or a dungeon. The knight finds his speech “strange and uncouth.”
evidence: Grammercy for thy courtesy, fair sir knight. The fact is, it's like this
Thy speech is strange and uncouth

questions.prompt: The knight believes the story of the enchanter until Robert says, “you're not real at all.” Why is that the part he cannot accept?
facilitatorNotes: Nobody wants to hear that he will vanish at sunset, and to the soldiers it sounds like madness or a trick to escape. Readers may find the moment funny, or a little sad, since Robert is telling the truth.
evidence: who seemed to have believed all the enchanter story till it came to his own share in it
the urchin doth but feign madness to escape from our clutches

questions.prompt: How does Robert win his freedom, and what does he forget when he makes his second wish?
facilitatorNotes: He appeals to the knight’s honor in the knight’s own style, and Sir Wulfric lets him go because he does not make war on children. At the sand-pit he wishes to be with the others but never thinks of wishing the castle and the siege away. Readers can decide which matters more, his quick thinking or his mistake.
evidence: should think foul scorn to--to keep a chap
Robert never thought of wishing the castle and the siege away.

readings.title: Five Children and It: no dinner (Chapter VI, end)
readings.challenge: Follow a character’s explanation of a puzzling magic rule, and test it against what you see.
readings.focus: Inside the castle there are no soldiers and no food, while the servants go on living in a house the children cannot see.
readings.context: Recap: while Robert was out, the others wished to be in a besieged castle. A knight’s army is camped outside and means to attack before sunset, when every wish ends. Robert talked his way free and wished himself back inside. The Lamb is the children’s baby brother, Martha their nursemaid. A gate-house guards a castle’s entrance; a portcullis is a heavy iron grating dropped to close the gate; a garrison is the soldiers who defend a castle, and provisioned means supplied with food. “Right as ninepence” means perfectly all right.
readings.contentNote: Jane says she feels “as if I was in a lunatic asylum,” an old and now hurtful name for a hospital for people with mental illness.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “A Castle and No Dinner,” from Robert’s return to the end of the chapter; opens “"We never heard you come in," they said. "How awfully jolly of you to wish it to give us…”; closes “Cyril tightened his belt ostentatiously. Jane burst into tears.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Robert less eager than the others to start shooting? What does he know that they don’t?
facilitatorNotes: He has been close to the soldiers and their weapons, and his ear is still sore from being dragged. The others have only looked at the camp from a window and think it is “as real as real” in a jolly way.
evidence: They're all quite, quite real.
I can feel my ear all sore yet.

questions.prompt: What is strange about Martha, the cook and the Lamb in the courtyard?
facilitatorNotes: Martha moves her hand back and forth, ironing on nothing; the cook puts an unseen dish into an invisible oven; the Lamb sits in the air, laughing. They are in the ordinary house, which the children cannot see.
evidence: the Lamb, who was sitting on nothing, about three feet from the ground, laughing happily
a-setting in his high chair as good as gold

questions.prompt: Retell Cyril’s explanation in your own words. Does Jane’s reply show that she doesn’t understand, or that she cares about something else?
facilitatorNotes: The servants never notice wishes, so they keep seeing the house; the castle stands in the same place, so the children see only the castle. Jane’s head swims, but she goes straight to the practical problem: an invisible dinner will be unfeelable too. She turns out to be right.
evidence: they can't see the castle, because they go on seeing the house
if it's invisible it'll be unfeelable as well, and then we can't eat it!

questions.prompt: How does each child react to the empty table? What does each reaction show about them?
facilitatorNotes: Robert, who did not care about dinner, now says it is the worst thing yet; Anthea makes the best of things “as usual”; Cyril tightens his belt for show; Jane bursts into tears. Readers can say which reaction they would share.
evidence: trying to make the best of things, as usual
Cyril tightened his belt ostentatiously. Jane burst into tears.

readings.title: Five Children and It: dinner out of the air (Chapter VII, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice how characters solve a problem by testing an idea, and how the mood changes as danger comes nearer.
readings.focus: The children find a way to eat their invisible dinner, then get ready to defend the castle.
readings.context: Five Children and It (1902) is by the English writer E. Nesbit. Cyril, Anthea (called Panther), Robert and Jane, with their baby brother the Lamb, are spending the summer in the Kent countryside, where they have dug up a Psammead: a grumpy, furry sand-fairy that grants one wish a day. Every wish lasts only until sunset. Today Cyril wished, while Robert was out, that they were in a besieged castle. An army led by the knight Sir Wulfric de Talbot is camped around it and means to attack before sunset. The servants cannot see the castle and go on living in the ordinary house, so the dinner Martha serves is invisible to the children. Squirrel is Cyril’s nickname. To reconnoitre is to look around to learn about an enemy; a battering-ram is a heavy log for breaking down doors; Bodiam Castle is a real castle in Sussex; javelins are throwing spears; a garrison is a castle’s defenders.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “A Siege and Bed,” from the opening until the biscuits are eaten at tea-time; opens “The children were sitting in the gloomy banqueting-hall, at the end of one of the long…”; closes “…putting by eight of the biscuits, in case anyone should feel faint in stress of battle.”.

questions.prompt: How does Cyril work out how to eat the dinner? What clue gives him the idea?
facilitatorNotes: The biscuits in his pocket stayed real because they already had them, so he guesses food becomes theirs once it is in their mouths. He bites at the air just above the table and comes up with bread.
evidence: unless it's because we had them
I suppose it isn't ours till we've got it in our mouths.

questions.prompt: The narrator says she will “draw a veil” over the meal. Why? What does she leave us to imagine?
facilitatorNotes: Picking mutton and suet pudding off a table with your mouth, “like a dog,” is messy and undignified. Refusing to describe it makes it funnier, and Martha’s remark about the mess tells the rest.
evidence: I think I will draw a veil over the rest of this painful scene
nobody looks nice picking up slices of suet pudding from the table in its mouth, like a dog

questions.prompt: Anthea asks Martha for “just biscuits for tea.” Why is that a clever idea?
facilitatorNotes: Food put into their pockets becomes theirs, so the air Martha crams into their pockets turns into biscuits, and the garrison has supplies until sunset.
evidence: four generous handfuls of air, which turned to biscuits

questions.prompt: Jane asks, “it is only a game, isn't it?” and no one answers. Why not? Are the others right to treat it as half a game?
facilitatorNotes: Robert has seen the soldiers close up and knows it is real; the others feel it is half make-believe, half a safe dream. The silence says what nobody wants to say aloud. Readers may think the others are wise not to frighten Jane, or that they are fooling themselves.
evidence: But no one answered.
none of them, except Robert, could feel all the time that this was real deadly dangerous work

readings.title: Five Children and It: the attack (Chapter VII, second part)
readings.challenge: Follow fast action in the right order, and notice how the characters argue about bravery.
readings.focus: The castle refuses to surrender, and the enemy finds a way across the moat.
readings.context: Recap: the children are shut in a magic castle besieged by Sir Wulfric de Talbot’s army until sunset. They ate their invisible dinner by biting it out of the air, filled their pockets with biscuits, and piled stones and daggers in the room over the gate. Pennoned lances carry small flags; “no quarter” means no mercy; a turret is a small tower; the drawbridge crosses the moat, and the portcullis is an iron gate that drops down behind it.
readings.contentNote: Robert hits a man’s fingers with an iron bar and the man falls back into the moat.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “A Siege and Bed,” from the trumpet call until the drawbridge comes down; opens “Just as he was putting away the reserve biscuits in a sort of little stone cupboard…”; closes “"Up--quick!" cried Robert,--"let's drop things on them."”.

questions.prompt: When the trumpet sounds, Anthea says Robert is brave. How do Cyril and Jane each answer?
facilitatorNotes: Cyril goes red and says Robert has had all afternoon to get ready and he himself will be braver “in half a jiffy”; Jane asks what it matters who is bravest and says she does not want to play.
evidence: He's been getting ready to be brave all the afternoon.
what does it matter which of you is the bravest?

questions.prompt: Anthea tells Jane that “civilised armies” spare women and children. Why isn’t Jane comforted?
facilitatorNotes: Jane sharply asks whether people from so long ago were civilised. Anthea is coaxing her little sister and points to the bright flags. Readers may think Jane has asked the better question, though Sir Wulfric did let Robert go.
evidence: the women and children are always spared by civilised armies
They seem to be such a long time ago.

questions.prompt: How does the army look and sound from the window? Why might Nesbit make it so pretty just before the attack?
facilitatorNotes: Green turf, white tents, bright flags and gleaming armour, with trumpets and the cling-clang of armour. The pretty picture hides the danger for a moment, so the attack that follows is more of a shock.
evidence: the scene was almost too pretty to be alarming
it was just like a splendid coloured picture

questions.prompt: Robert locks Jakin in the upper room. Why does the drawbridge come down anyway?
facilitatorNotes: Jakin has swum the moat and is already in the room with the drawbridge machinery; locking the door shuts him in with it. Robert stopped him escaping, not working the bridge.
evidence: he was fiddling about with the machinery which Robert felt sure worked the drawbridge
That's that beast Jakin

readings.title: Five Children and It: sunset (Chapter VII, end)
readings.challenge: Decide how a character changes in a crisis, and enjoy a joke that turns on cause and effect.
readings.focus: The siege ends at sunset, but one thing from the castle comes home with them.
readings.context: Recap: Cyril’s wish put the children in a castle besieged by Sir Wulfric de Talbot’s army until sunset. The attackers have crossed the moat, lowered the drawbridge and begun to batter the great door. A parley is a talk with the enemy under a flag of truce; the Civil Service means government office work; the lead-holes were for pouring boiling lead on attackers; an arrow-slit is a narrow window for shooting through. Martha is the nursemaid, and she is proud of her new cap.
readings.contentNote: The children drop stones on the attackers and hear groans; Robert says he hopes they have hurt somebody.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “A Siege and Bed,” from the stones dropped on the attackers to the end of the chapter; opens “Even the girls were feeling almost brave now. They followed Robert quickly, and under his…”; closes “…Yes--frightfully. Do stand still--you're only tightening the knot," said Anthea.”.

questions.prompt: Anthea is sorry they may have hurt someone, but Robert says, “I should hope we had!” What does the narrator call him, and how has he changed since the morning?
facilitatorNotes: She calls him “the bloodthirsty Robert.” In the morning he could not even think of a wish; now he wants boiling lead, will never surrender and means to be a soldier. Readers may admire his courage or think the game has carried him away.
evidence: said the bloodthirsty Robert
Oh, I'll be a soldier when I grow up

questions.prompt: What happens at the moment of sunset? How does Nesbit make the change feel sudden?
facilitatorNotes: Every noise stops at once, “like the snuff of a candle,” the room whirls, and they are in their own front bedroom. One long sentence carries them from the battle to the ugly iron roof of the house.
evidence: went out like the snuff of a candle
safe and sound, in the big front bedroom of their own house

questions.prompt: Anthea says this is the first wish that has not got them into a row. What happens next, and why is the timing funny?
facilitatorNotes: Martha bursts in at once: someone has emptied water on her head on the front doorstep. Jane guesses that the castle well was their own well in the stable-yard, so the water stayed real when the castle vanished. The row arrives the moment Anthea says there will not be one.
evidence: This is the very first thing we've wished for that hasn't got us into a row.
you must be emptying the water jug on their heads!

questions.prompt: Jane says, “I wasn't frightened a bit.” Is she telling the truth? What might she mean?
facilitatorNotes: Earlier she begged to surrender. Now that she is safe she may be boasting, or the fear may feel different once it is over. Anthea stops Cyril from arguing, which is kind. Readers can decide.
evidence: "Oh, it was simply splendid!" said Jane unexpectedly. "I wasn't frightened a bit."
don't you think we'd better surrender?

readings.title: Five Children and It: the Lamb grows up (Chapter IX, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice how a cross sentence turns into a wish, and how the narrator slows the change down so that we watch it happen.
readings.focus: Cyril persuades the Psammead to grant wishes wherever the children are, and his own temper turns the baby into a young man.
readings.context: Five Children and It (1902) is by the English writer E. Nesbit. Cyril, Anthea (called Panther), Robert and Jane, with their baby brother the Lamb, are spending the summer in the Kent countryside, where they have dug up a Psammead: a grumpy, furry sand-fairy that grants one wish a day. Every wish lasts only until sunset. In the last adventure Robert wished to be bigger than the baker’s boy and spent a day as a giant at a fair. Water hurts the Psammead, so Robert’s tears upset it. A Megatherium is a giant ground sloth of long ago; a Waterbury was a cheap American watch; a smock is a loose child’s garment; flannels are the light suit young men wore for summer sports, and a straw hat went with them.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Grown Up,” from the opening until the grown-up Lamb lies down to sleep under the chestnut tree; opens “Cyril had once pointed out that ordinary life is full of occasions on which a wish would…”; closes “…pale green necktie like the other Lamb? or had his mind grown up together with his body?”.

questions.prompt: What does Cyril ask the Psammead for? Why does the narrator call him “crafty”?
facilitatorNotes: He asks for wishes to be granted “just when we think of it, and just where we happen to be,” and pretends it is so the children need not disturb the Psammead again. The real reason is their own convenience. The Psammead warns that it will end in a wish they do not really want.
evidence: won't you let us have our wish just when we think of it, and just where we happen to be?
added the crafty Cyril

questions.prompt: How does the wish slip out? Is the Lamb the only one to blame for Cyril’s bad mood?
facilitatorNotes: The Lamb kicks and breaks the glass of father’s second-best watch, and Cyril says crossly, “I wish to goodness he would--grow up now!” But Cyril had borrowed the watch “without leave,” and the Lamb is two. Anthea’s warning comes out at the same moment, too late.
evidence: which Cyril had borrowed without leave
like music to a song her words and Cyril's came out together

questions.prompt: Which details of the change does the narrator choose? Why is the mustache “most terrible of all”?
facilitatorNotes: The face changes first: thinner, lined, darker eyes, a longer mouth, while the body is still a baby’s in a smock and socks. A mustache on a two-year-old is funny and horrible at once, which is the feeling of the whole chapter.
evidence: most terrible of all, a little dark mustache appeared on the lip
a two-year-old baby in a linen smock and white open-work socks

questions.prompt: The part ends with a question: has the Lamb’s mind grown up with his body? Which answer would be worse for the children? Predict.
facilitatorNotes: If he is grown up inside he will not let them look after him; if he is still a baby inside, nobody can manage a baby in a man’s body. Either way they must get him home. One clue: the new Lamb goes to sleep at an odd time, as the baby always did.
evidence: or had his mind grown up together with his body?
The Lamb--the original little tiresome beloved Lamb often went to sleep at odd times

readings.title: Five Children and It: Hilary, St. Maur or Devereux (Chapter IX, second part)
readings.challenge: Work out what the children really want while they say something else, and notice when they begin to deceive.
readings.focus: The grown-up Lamb is a lofty young man who wants nothing to do with his brothers and sisters, so they must trick him into staying.
readings.context: Recap: cross that the Lamb had broken a watch, Cyril wished by accident that the baby would grow up at once. Now a young man in a flannel suit with a little black mustache is asleep under a chestnut tree, and the wish lasts until sunset. Maidstone and Rochester are towns in Kent; a club is a London gentlemen’s club where men lunched; “grub” and a “blow-out” are slang for food and a big meal; brake-fern is bracken; Anthea’s pin held her skirt to her bodice, the top of her dress. Robert earned fifteen shillings as a giant at a fair.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Grown Up,” from the children’s council in the fern to the mending of the eighteenth puncture; opens “That was the question which the others, in a hurried council held among the yellowing…”; closes “…up from the completed work with a sigh of relief, and suddenly put his tie straight.”.

questions.prompt: How does the grown-up Lamb talk to the others when he wakes? Find words that show he now thinks of them as little children.
facilitatorNotes: “Hullo, kiddies!”, “cut along home,” “little girls should be seen and not heard,” and a penny “if you’re good.” He talks like a bored older brother; the joke is that the baby they look after is now bossing them.
evidence: "Hullo, kiddies!" he said in a languid tone
little girls should be seen and not heard

questions.prompt: Why does the thought of the Lamb lunching at a London club nearly make Anthea cry?
facilitatorNotes: She sees past sunset: he will turn back into “a helpless cross sleepy baby” among strangers, crying for her (“Panty” is his name for Anthea). The others worry about getting into trouble; Anthea worries about him.
evidence: a helpless cross sleepy baby would find itself alone amid unsympathetic waiters
The picture moved Anthea almost to tears.

questions.prompt: The narrator says the wishes were making the children “wise beyond their years.” What tricks do they use, and are they honest ones?
facilitatorNotes: Anthea calls him “Dear Hilary” and says father would not like it; Cyril tries a “man to man” tone; Robert punctures the tyres with Anthea’s pin, and Anthea holds up a thorn as if it caused them. Anthea and Robert both notice they are deceiving. Readers can weigh this against the danger of losing a baby.
evidence: Oh, deceitful thing that I am!
wondering how he could so soon have learned to deceive

questions.prompt: Why is it “really rather noble of Cyril” to ask to go with the Lamb?
facilitatorNotes: Cyril never liked being seen in public with the Lamb, and this Lamb will become a baby again at sunset, wherever he is. Cyril also admits the trouble is his own doing, so he takes on the hardest part.
evidence: This was really rather noble of Cyril
Yes, I know it's my doing; don't rub it in!

readings.title: Five Children and It: the young lady with the bicycle (Chapter IX, end)
readings.challenge: Follow a running joke that the narrator keeps changing, and decide why she keeps it up.
readings.focus: To stop the Lamb riding off with a stranger, the children make a scene, and sunset gives them back their baby.
readings.context: Recap: grown up for a day by an accidental wish, the Lamb wants to leave his brothers and sisters behind. They have kept him near by secretly puncturing his bicycle tyres, and he has spent the afternoon mending them at a cottage that serves teas to cyclists. A swill pail holds kitchen scraps for pigs; “mad as hatters” is an old saying; “bremmink” is the Lamb’s baby word for bread and milk. The Psammead arranged that servants never notice what the wishes change.
readings.contentNote: The young lady calls the children “dangerous lunatics” and Anthea “a maniac,” old words for madness; Cyril jokes about bullying his baby brother.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Grown Up,” from the arrival of the young lady to the end of the chapter; opens “"There's a lady coming," he said briskly,--"for goodness' sake, get out of the way. Go…”; closes “"Me loves Panty--wants to come to own Panty!"”.

questions.prompt: The narrator keeps calling the Lamb by different names: Hilary, St. Maur, Devereux, and at last none at all. What joke is she making?
facilitatorNotes: The grown-up Lamb insisted on his grand names, so the narrator pretends to obey and keeps getting it wrong or changing her mind, which makes fun of his self-importance. At the end she buries the names “in oblivion,” as the baby comes back.
evidence: the grown-up Lamb (sometimes called St. Maur in these pages)
whose names shall now be buried in oblivion

questions.prompt: When the lady asks who the dirty children are, the Lamb says he does not know. Why does Jane’s true answer make things worse?
facilitatorNotes: He is ashamed of them, and the narrator says he “lied miserably.” Jane tells the plain truth, a baby brother under a spell, and the truth sounds madder than any lie; the lady rides off and tells her family she escaped from lunatics.
evidence: "I don't know," he lied miserably.
our own little baby brother that we're so fond of

questions.prompt: How does Martha see the Lamb, and why will the children never forget the sight?
facilitatorNotes: Martha cannot see the change, so she scoops up what she thinks is the baby. The children see a young man in a flannel suit with a mustache struggling in her arms while she promises him his bread and milk. After his rudeness all day, it is a comic kind of justice.
evidence: the servants in the house should never notice any change
struggling in the sturdy arms of Martha

questions.prompt: At the end the children disagree about how to bring up the Lamb. Which view do you agree with, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Cyril would bully him for his own good; Anthea refuses; Jane would “tame him by kindness”; Robert says the trouble was growing up with no time to improve. Anthea says he needs no improving, and the baby’s voice gets the last word. Any view can be argued from the chapter.
evidence: We must tame him by kindness
There was no time to improve him at all.

readings.title: Five Children and It: Jane’s wish (Chapter XI, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice what the narrator tells you that the children do not know, and how that changes the way you read.
readings.focus: Wanting to please their mother, the children are careful all morning, until Jane wishes aloud without meaning to.
readings.context: Five Children and It (1902) is by the English writer E. Nesbit. Cyril, Anthea (called Panther), Robert and Jane, with their baby brother the Lamb, are spending the summer in the Kent countryside, where they have dug up a Psammead: a grumpy, furry sand-fairy that grants one wish a day. Every wish lasts only until sunset. Since Cyril’s bargain with the Psammead, a wish comes true wherever the children happen to say “I wish.” Their mother has been away looking after Granny. Florins were two-shilling coins; Peasemarsh Place is a big house near by; a “river” of diamonds is a long necklace of them, and a tiara is a jewelled band worn on the head; a receiver of stolen goods keeps things that were stolen. Martha is the nursemaid, and Beale a gamekeeper.
readings.contentNote: Cyril frightens Jane with a picture of a “mad-house,” drawn from old, cruel ideas about mental illness.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, “The Last Wish,” from the opening until the children fill the house with flowers; opens “Of course you, who see above that this is the eleventh (and last) chapter, know very well…”; closes “…late red roses from the wall of the stableyard, till the house was a perfect bower.”.

questions.prompt: The narrator begins by telling you something the children do not know. What is it, and how does it change the way you read?
facilitatorNotes: This is the last chapter, so it is their last day of wishes. We read their plans knowing they will not last; even their sudden “beautiful and sensible ideas” come too late. Jane’s “This is always the way” is funnier because we know.
evidence: know very well that the day of which this chapter tells must be the last
But the children themselves did not know this.

questions.prompt: Why do the children decide the day’s wish must please their mother? What does Cyril say against Jane’s idea?
facilitatorNotes: Mother is coming home that afternoon, so they want a wish for her, not themselves. Jane says she would like them to be good; Cyril says that is dull, and that they should manage it without a sand-fairy’s help.
evidence: the wish of the day must be something to please mother and not to please themselves
I should hope we could be that without sand-fairies to help us

questions.prompt: How does Jane’s wish slip out? Is it fair to blame her?
facilitatorNotes: She is daydreaming aloud about finding the jewels for mother and says “I wish she would” without meaning it as a wish. Anthea had just warned them. The others are horrified, but Robert says they will stand by her.
evidence: rings and everything in her room when she came home. I wish she would
We'll stand by you.

questions.prompt: Their father says you need never be afraid if you speak the truth. Why don’t Cyril and Anthea think the truth will help this time?
facilitatorNotes: Once before they told the police the truth about the Psammead, and nobody believed it. Anthea puts it neatly: it is true, but “not true enough for grown-up people to believe.” Readers can discuss whether that means they should still tell it.
evidence: They remembered how convincing the truth about the Psammead had been once before when told to the police.
it's not true enough for grown-up people to believe it

readings.title: Five Children and It: jewels in mother’s room (Chapter XI, second part)
readings.challenge: Watch the children try to say only true things in a scene where the whole truth cannot be told.
readings.focus: Mother finds the stolen jewels, an innocent man falls under suspicion, and she sets off for the police.
readings.context: Recap: on the day their mother is coming home, Jane wished by accident that Lady Chittenden’s stolen jewels would be in their mother’s room. The children could not find the Psammead to undo it, and fear nobody will believe the truth. Servants cannot see what the wishes change. To give warning is to give notice of leaving a job; a gamekeeper looks after the animals on an estate; a trap is a light carriage; Rochester is the nearest town; felons are criminals.
readings.contentNote: Martha calls the other servant, Eliza, “a slut,” which then meant an untidy, dirty woman and is now an offensive insult. The children again picture a “mad-house” with cruel old ideas about mental illness.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, “The Last Wish,” from mother’s return until Robert sits miserably in the garden; opens “And almost as soon as dinner was cleared away mother arrived, and was clasped in eight…”; closes “…sat down on the worn yellow grass, with his miserable head between his helpless hands.”.

questions.prompt: When mother asks where the ring came from, each child says “I don't know” “truthfully.” Why does the narrator add that word?
facilitatorNotes: It is true that they do not know how the ring got there, but they know far more than they say. Then Jane tells the whole truth (“We found a Fairy”) and is told not to talk nonsense. The scene plays with the difference between a true answer and the whole truth.
evidence: "I don't know," said each of the children truthfully.
"We found a Fairy," said Jane obediently.

questions.prompt: How does Cyril steer the talk away from Jane? Does he lie?
facilitatorNotes: He says they have never seen the jewels before and suggests they are Lady Chittenden’s, both true. Then he nearly says “sunset” and changes it to “nightfall.” He misleads without quite lying; readers can judge whether that is better.
evidence: we've never seen the things before
they thought it better to wait for--for sunset--nightfall, I mean

questions.prompt: Martha’s confession makes things worse for Beale. Why are the children so upset?
facilitatorNotes: She admits that Beale helped her clean the windows, so he will be suspected of the robbery. Jane’s wish has put an innocent man in danger, and the children feel they cannot tell the truth that would clear him.
evidence: Here was an innocent man accused of robbery through that silly wish of Jane's
He's a great dear; he is, truly and honourably, and as honest as the day.

questions.prompt: Cyril calls their mother “a born general.” What does she do to earn the name, and why does it make their trouble worse?
facilitatorNotes: She acts at once: locks the jewels away, posts Cyril and Robert on guard, arranges for the farm men, and sets off for the police. Her quickness, like Anthea’s, leaves no time for the children to put things right before sunset.
evidence: When she had set her mind on a thing she always went straight through with it
"She's a born general," said Cyril

readings.title: Five Children and It: the last wish (Chapter XI, end)
readings.challenge: Watch a familiar character show a new side, and judge whether a bargain is fair to both sides.
readings.focus: Anthea finds the Psammead and makes a bargain: as many wishes as it can manage today, and never another.
readings.context: Recap: Jane’s accidental wish put a lady’s stolen jewels in their mother’s room. Mother has locked them up and gone to tell the police, and an innocent gamekeeper, Beale, may be blamed. Cocoanut matting is a rough floor mat; a forlorn hope is a last desperate try. The Psammead’s “dull things” were real reforms argued about in 1902: taxes that rise with income, pensions for old people, votes for all men, and free schooling for older children; Nesbit belonged to the Fabian Society, which campaigned for such changes. The Brass Bottle is a comic novel of the time in which a genie’s wishes have to be undone.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, “The Last Wish,” from Anthea and Jane’s whispered talk to the end of the book; opens “Anthea and Jane whispered together in the passage downstairs, where the cocoanut matting…”; closes “…but in a very, very, very different place. It was in a---- But I must say no more.”.

questions.prompt: How does Anthea persuade the Psammead? What did Jane notice that gave her the idea?
facilitatorNotes: Jane says she believes the Psammead hates giving wishes. Anthea catches it gently but firmly and offers what it wants most: never to be asked again after today.
evidence: I believe he hates having to give wishes.
If you'll only do what we want to-day, we'll never ask you for another wish as long as we live.

questions.prompt: List the wishes in order. How does each one untie part of the trouble?
facilitatorNotes: Lady Chittenden never lost her jewels; mother does not reach the police; mother forgets the diamonds; Martha forgets the ring and mother forgets Beale at the windows, so nobody suspects him. Then the children wish the Psammead’s own wish, and a kind goodbye.
evidence: I wish Lady Chittenden may find she's never lost her jewels.
I wish Martha to forget about the diamond ring, and mother to forget about the keeper cleaning the windows.

questions.prompt: Why does the Psammead not want grown-ups to know about it? Do you agree that their wishes would be “dull”?
facilitatorNotes: Grown-ups would wish “real earnest things,” and scientists might make wishes last past sunset, so the world would be “topsy-turvy.” The joke is that the dull things are serious reforms that could change many lives. Readers can decide whether the Psammead or the grown-ups are right.
evidence: they wouldn't wish silly things like you do, but real earnest things
the whole world would be turned topsy-turvy

questions.prompt: The book ends with Robert saying, “I never want to.” Have the wishes been good for the children or not? Use this chapter.
facilitatorNotes: Every wish brought trouble, and Robert has had enough. But the children have learned to think fast, to be careful, and to be kind: Anthea thanks the Psammead and wishes it a good sleep. Jane hopes to see it again, and the narrator promises they will.
evidence: I hope we shall see you again some day
"I never want to," said Robert earnestly.
